name: Amok
title: Priestly Head after the Exile
summary: Amok was the head of a priestly family in Jerusalem after returning from the Babylonian exile. He is mentioned in Nehemiah 12 among the priests and Levites who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel and the high priest Joshua. In the next generation, under the high priest Joiakim, it was Eber who represented Amok's family as its head. The fact that Amok is listed in the priestly genealogies testifies to the careful documentation of priestly lineage, which was essential for maintaining the legitimacy of temple service in the restored community. Through his role as head of the priestly line, Amok helped ensure continuity in Israel's worship life after the exile.

keyEvents.title: The Lineage of Amok under High Priest Joiakim

versions.summary: Amok was a priest or head of a priestly family who returned to Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. He is mentioned in the book of Nehemiah as one of the priestly leaders who served under high priest Joiakim. He represents the faithful rebuilding of Israel's religious life after returning from Babylon.

versions.reason: [major] In Nehemiah 12:20, Eber is mentioned as the head of the priestly family of Amok during the time of Joiakim. This does not necessarily mean that Eber was Amok's biological son – he was rather the head of the priestly family or clan bearing the name Amok. The relationship should still be retained since it is the closest available information, but this should be noted in footnotes.; [minor] The third key event ('Part of the rebuilding of the priesthood') is somewhat generic and overlaps with the first event. The verses (Neh 12:1,7) provide context, but verse 1 does not mention Amok directly – it serves as an introduction to the list. This could be simplified or merged with the first event.; [minor] The fourth key event ('Registration of priestly families') overlaps with event 2. Neh 12:12 is the introduction to the list of priestly heads under Joiakim, while verse 20 mentions Amok specifically. This event can be combined with event 2 to avoid repetition.; [minor] The role 'priestly head' or 'leader of a priestly family' could have been added in addition to 'priest', to reflect the title and better describe Amok's function.; [major] The profile lacks footnotes. Information should be added about the priestly organization after the exile, the significance of genealogical records, and possibly the linguistic background of the name Amok.

Amok is part of the faithful rebuilding of Israel's religious institutions after returning from Babylon, and his record in the priestly genealogies confirms the family's legitimate place in temple service.

footnotes.text: The name Amok (Hebrew: עָמוֹק, 'Amoq) may mean 'deep' or 'profound'. It is a rare name in the Hebrew Bible and occurs only in Nehemiah 12.

The lists in Nehemiah 12 of priestly lineages served an important function in the post-exilic community: they documented the legitimacy of the priestly families who served in the rebuilt temple. Such registration was crucial to ensure that only those with proper ancestry could perform priestly duties (cf. Ezra 2:62).

The term 'head' (Hebrew: רֹאשׁ, rosh) for the priestly families indicates that the priesthood after the exile was organized into lineage-based divisions, similar to the system attributed to David in 1 Chronicles 24. Each division had a head who represented the lineage.

Eber, mentioned as the head of Amok's lineage in the time of Joiakim (Neh 12:20), likely represents the next generation of the priestly family. In the post-exilic system, the leadership role in the priestly line often passed from father to son, even though the family name was preserved after its founder.

The return from Babylon under Zerubbabel is traditionally dated to around 538–520 BC. The priestly lineage lists in Nehemiah 12 cover several generations, from this first return up to Nehemiah's own time, providing a rare insight into the continuity of the Israelite priesthood over a period of more than a hundred years.

The Hebrew verb with the same root as Amok (ע-מ-ק) is also used figuratively in the Bible for something unfathomable or difficult to understand (cf. Ps 92:6; Eccl 7:24), making the name theologically interesting in a priestly context.
